sections.h2: What does the Coconino County Recorder do when a house sells?
sections.html:
The County Recorder takes in the deed that moves title to a buyer and puts it on the public record, along with the mortgage releases and liens that affect the house. In Coconino County those records belong to the Flagstaff office, and the county's online records portal lists Treasurer, Assessor, GIS and Recorder links side by side.

Most sellers never visit the counter. A title or escrow company prepares the deed, gathers signatures, pays the fee and records it. Still, a seller who knows what the office requires can catch errors, particularly on inherited or family transfers where paperwork is handled by hand.

sections.h2: What does Arizona law say a recorder may charge?
sections.html:
Arizona sets recorder fees in A.R.S. 11-475, and the base charge for most documents is $30 per instrument. The figures below come straight from that statute.

ServiceFee
Papers required or authorized by law to be recorded, unless the fee is set elsewhere$30 per instrument
Papers recorded at the request of the United States, the state or a local government that is a party$15 per instrument
Preparing and certifying a copy$1 per page or partial page
Recorder's certificate and seal on a copy$3 more
Certificate under section 47-9523$10 per name, plus $1 per financing statement or assignment listed

The $30 and $15 charges already include an amount collected under another section, 11-475.01. Copies for a state agency's official use cost half the usual fee, and the recorder collects nothing from the county office where the document is to be recorded when public money would pay the fee. The recorder also charges no fee to record or release a restitution lien or a lien to enforce a support order.

Read the full fee statute if you need an official figure, since the Coconino County Recorder's counter may post a current schedule.

sections.h2: What is an affidavit of legal value, and who signs it?
sections.html:
Most deeds that transfer title, and contracts for the sale of real property, must carry an affidavit of legal value signed by buyer and seller, or by an agent of either (A.R.S. 11-1133). It uses a form approved by the Arizona Department of Revenue. The recorder must refuse to record a deed without a complete affidavit unless the instrument notes a statutory exemption.

The affidavit collects the facts about the sale:

  • Names, mailing addresses and phone numbers of buyer and seller.
  • The address where a tax statement should go.
  • The legal description, the street address and the date of sale.
  • The total price, any cash down payment and the type of financing: cash, a new third-party loan, a seller loan, an assumption, or an exchange.
  • Whether personal property worth five percent or more of the price changed hands.
  • The assessor's parcel number.
  • The conditions of the sale, including any relationship between the parties.
  • How the property is used and, for a house, whether it will be owner-occupied or rented.

An affidavit counts as complete when each item is answered or marked not applicable. Leaving a line blank is a common reason for a rejected recording.

sections.h2: Does a house sale in Coconino County pay a transfer tax?
sections.html:
The exemption statute does mention "the affidavit and fee required by this article," which means the affidavit itself carries a fee. Ask the County Recorder or the Arizona Department of Revenue for the current amount.

Instead of guessing, ask your escrow officer to itemize every recording charge on the settlement statement. The Coconino County recording line should show the $30 base fee per instrument, or a higher total if several documents are recorded together, such as a deed and a release of a prior lien.

sections.h2: What format rules can get a Coconino County document rejected?
sections.html:
A.R.S. 11-480 lets a recorder reject only an instrument that fails a short list of formal tests at the counter. A caption describing the instrument is required, such as warranty deed. It must be an original with original signatures, legible enough to copy, and no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches with type no smaller than ten point.

The first page needs a two inch top margin reserved for recording information, and the other margins need to be at least half an inch. If the first page does not meet the top margin rule, the person recording attaches a separate cover sheet with the title of the document. A document that changes an earlier recorded paper must cite the earlier recording date and its docket and page.

Once a recorder accepts an instrument, a later claim that it breached these rules cannot invalidate it.

sections.h2: What do you need to know about Coconino County before listing a house?
sections.html:
Coconino County covers 18,661 square miles, with Flagstaff as county seat and largest city, and a 2020 census count of 145,101 people. Of the county's 69,108 housing units, 25.7 percent were vacant and 59.2 percent of the occupied units were owned by their occupants.

A few Coconino County facts that can shape a sale:

  • The county was formed in 1891, with Flagstaff as its seat.
  • Interstate 40 and Interstate 17 meet at Flagstaff, and Amtrak and commercial flights serve the city.
  • Northern Arizona University is the biggest employer on a 2017 list, with 3,500 workers, ahead of W. L. Gore and Associates and Flagstaff Medical Center.
  • Reservation land covers 7,142 square miles of the county, so ask your title company about any parcel near it.

Within the county, a sale of a Flagstaff bungalow, a Page rental or a Williams cabin follows the same state recording steps. The Recorder at 110 East Cherry Avenue handles the filing, and the title company usually does the rest.

sections.h2: Where do you get a tax balance before recording a Coconino County deed?
sections.html:
The Coconino County Treasurer is at 110 E. Cherry Avenue in Flagstaff, with hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. You can reach the office at (928) 679-8188, toll free at (877) 500-1818, or at treasurer@coconino.az.gov.

Tax is a lien from January 1 of the tax year, so the balance should be known before the deed is recorded. Escrow normally pays the Treasurer from the seller's proceeds at closing, and then the deed is submitted to the Recorder.

sections.h2: Who records documents on behalf of an out-of-town seller?
sections.html: Most recordings are submitted by the escrow or title company, which also pays the fee. If you plan to handle a family or estate transfer yourself, call the Recorder first and ask which forms the office wants. Statute requires original signatures on a recorded instrument, so a photocopy of a signed deed will not do.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Coconino County?
faqs.a: Arizona's fee statute sets $30 per instrument for most recorded papers, and the county page for Coconino lists the same flat fee for basic recordings. Government parties pay $15 per instrument when they ask for the recording.

faqs.q: What is an affidavit of legal value in Arizona?
faqs.a: It is a form signed by buyer and seller, or their agents, that gives the price, financing type, parcel number and other facts about a sale. The recorder must reject a deed without it unless the deed cites an exemption.

faqs.q: Does a gift deed need the affidavit in Arizona?
faqs.a: No. A deed of gift is on the exemption list in A.R.S. 11-1134, and the instrument has to state the exemption on its face. Check with the Recorder or a title company before relying on it.

faqs.q: What size and margins must a recorded document have?
faqs.a: A recorded instrument can be no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, with type of at least ten point, a two inch top margin on page one and half inch margins elsewhere. A cover sheet can fix a first page that falls short.

faqs.q: Where is the Coconino County Recorder?
faqs.a: The office is at 110 East Cherry Avenue, first floor, in Flagstaff, with weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., according to the county listing summarized on this page. Call before visiting to confirm.
